title: Job 27:1–12
context: The narrator introduces a further speech: “Job again took up his parable” (27:1). The new introduction, coming where a third speech from Zophar might be expected, marks Job as the speaker in the book as it stands. Job swears an oath by the life of God, “who has taken away my right” (27:2), declaring that while breath remains in him he will not speak unrighteousness or deceit (27:3–4). He refuses to concede that the friends are right and vows to hold fast to his integrity and righteousness as long as he lives (27:5–6). He then wishes that his enemy be as the wicked and asks what hope the godless have when God takes away their life (27:7–10), before promising to teach the friends about the hand of God and asking why they have become “altogether vain” (27:11–12). Job’s claim of righteousness is not a claim to sinlessness but a refusal to confess guilt for sins that would explain his suffering; the narrator and God himself have called him blameless (1:1, 8; 2:3). Both Arminian and Reformed readers hear in the oath a striking mixture of protest and faith: Job accuses God of denying him justice, yet swears by God’s life and appeals to no one else. Neither tradition treats the protest as the book’s final word, which comes in the LORD’s speeches and Job’s response (38–42), and neither condemns Job’s honesty here.

verses.text: Job again took up his parable, and said,
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator introduces a new speech with “Job again took up his parable,” a formula used again in 29:1. Arminian readers note that the absence of a third speech from Zophar leaves Job holding the floor, and they see the change of formula as a sign that the dialogue with the friends is giving way to Job’s closing defense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the new formula and the missing third speech from Zophar, and they observe that the book now moves toward Job’s final protest (29–31) and the LORD’s answer. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as marking Job as the speaker in the text as it stands, while recognizing that readers debate the structure of the third cycle.

verses.text: “As God lives, who has taken away my right, the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter
verses.arminianNotes: Job swears by the living God, “who has taken away my right,” and by the Almighty, who has made his soul bitter. Arminian readers hear real protest against God, yet they stress that Job swears by God and no other, so that his complaint is still addressed within a relationship he will not abandon, as his earlier hope also showed (19:25–27).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the paradox that Job blames God for his loss of justice while appealing to God as the guarantor of his oath. They see faith persevering beneath bitter words, and they hold that God’s purposes in Job’s suffering remain good though hidden (compare 1:8–12). Shared ground: both traditions read the oath as protest within faith, not as apostasy.

verses.text: (for the length of my life is still in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils);
verses.arminianNotes: Job adds that the length of his life is still in him and the spirit of God is in his nostrils, recalling God’s breath of life (compare Genesis 2:7). Arminian readers see Job confessing that every breath he has is God’s gift, even as he protests, and they note how deeply his oath is rooted in dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear Job acknowledging that God sustains his life moment by moment, a theme Elihu later echoes (33:4). They see in the confession a sign that Job’s protest never becomes a denial of God as Creator and sustainer. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a confession of creaturely dependence set within Job’s oath.

verses.text: surely my lips will not speak unrighteousness, neither will my tongue utter deceit.
verses.arminianNotes: Job swears that his lips will not speak unrighteousness and his tongue will not utter deceit. Arminian readers see a man who values truth so highly that he will not lie even to end his suffering, and they hear in his resolve the kind of genuine integrity that God praised in the prologue (1:8; 2:3).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job refuses to confess sins he has not committed simply to satisfy the friends’ theology, and they see this as faithfulness to the truth rather than pride. Shared ground: both traditions hold that honesty before God is better than a false confession, and both read Job’s resolve as integrity rather than a claim to sinless perfection.

verses.text: Far be it from me that I should justify you. Until I die I will not put away my integrity from me.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says, “Far be it from me that I should justify you,” and vows not to put away his integrity until he dies. Arminian readers stress that Job will not agree that the friends are right, because doing so would mean confessing guilt he does not have, and they admire his refusal to abandon the truth under pressure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear Job holding to the same integrity his wife urged him to give up (2:9) and the LORD affirmed (2:3). They note that integrity here means wholehearted devotion, not sinlessness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s refusal to accept the friends’ verdict, without treating every word of his protest as beyond correction (compare 42:3).

verses.text: I hold fast to my righteousness, and will not let it go. My heart will not reproach me so long as I live.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says he holds fast to his righteousness and his heart will not reproach him while he lives. Arminian readers see a sincere conscience that knows its own faithfulness, and they stress that God genuinely values the obedience of those who walk with him, as the prologue shows, even while all depend on his grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers take Job’s righteousness here as the integrity of a godly life, not a claim to merit justification before God, and they note that Job will later humble himself before the LORD (40:4; 42:6). Shared ground: both traditions agree that Job is not claiming sinlessness, and both read his clear conscience as honest testimony within faith.

verses.text: “Let my enemy be as the wicked. Let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous.
verses.arminianNotes: Job wishes that his enemy be as the wicked and his opponent as the unrighteous. Some readers think Job is hinting that the friends, by accusing him falsely, put themselves in the place of the wicked. Arminian readers hear a cry for justice rather than personal vengeance, set within Job’s confidence that God will vindicate the innocent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel with imprecatory language in the Psalms, where the righteous ask God to deal justly with their enemies (compare Psalm 109), and they read it as an appeal for God’s justice. Who the enemy is remains debated. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as an appeal for justice, not as a model for personal revenge.

verses.text: For what is the hope of the godless, when he is cut off, when God takes away his life?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks what hope the godless have when they are cut off and God takes away their life. Arminian readers note that Job, unlike the godless, still looks to God for vindication, and they see a contrast between a hope that rests in God and one that ends at death, which shows Job’s faith despite his complaints.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job distinguishing his own case from the godless, whose hope perishes, and they connect the verse with the wider biblical teaching that hope beyond death rests in God alone (compare 19:25–27). Shared ground: both traditions read the question as Job affirming that he is not godless, even while he protests his suffering.

verses.text: Will God hear his cry when trouble comes on him?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether God will hear the cry of the godless when trouble comes. Arminian readers note the implied contrast: Job keeps calling on God and expects to be heard eventually, which distinguishes him from the godless, and they see in this a faith that persists through apparent silence from heaven.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear Job implying that the godless have no claim on God’s ear in trouble, while Job himself still seeks a hearing (compare 23:3–7). They see faith persevering through perplexity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as contrasting Job’s ongoing appeal to God with the hopelessness of those who reject him.

verses.text: Will he delight himself in the Almighty, and call on God at all times?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether the godless will delight themselves in the Almighty and call on God at all times. Arminian readers see Job describing what genuine faith looks like, delighting in God and calling on him continually, and they note that his whole speech shows him doing exactly that even in his pain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that delight in God and constant prayer are marks of true faith (compare Psalm 37:4), and they see Job implying that such marks belong to him, not to the godless. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing living faith, and both see Job’s persistence in calling on God as evidence of it.

verses.text: I will teach you about the hand of God. I will not conceal that which is with the Almighty.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says he will teach the friends about the hand of God and not conceal what is with the Almighty. Arminian readers see Job reversing the roles: the friends have tried to instruct him, and now he offers to instruct them, drawing on his own wrestling with God rather than on received tradition alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear Job claiming to understand God’s ways at least as well as the friends, while noting that the LORD later shows that Job too has spoken beyond his knowledge (38:2; 42:3). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s confident claim, leaving the book’s later speeches to weigh it.

verses.text: Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?
verses.arminianNotes: Job tells the friends that they have all seen the matter themselves, yet they have become altogether vain. Arminian readers note that Job appeals to shared experience, perhaps of the prosperity of the wicked described in chapter 21, and charges the friends with empty words that do not match what they have observed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job rebuking the friends for drawing false conclusions from what they know, and they note that the book later confirms that the friends did not speak rightly about God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s charge that the friends’ theology has become empty when applied to his case.
